_purpose: Non-contractual delivery parameters the schedule and queue compute against.
_why_separate: None of this is in the signed agreement. Capacity is what the consultant can commit; the agreement fixes dates and hours. Keeping them apart stops a capacity assumption being read as a contractual term.
capacity_source: D-6, docs/Import/baseline-lock.yml — 'I can commit 16 hours a week physically, but use AI to deploy so move much more work.'
estimating_rule_meaning: Billable hours are the WBS estimate for the scope actually DELIVERED, not elapsed time. Completion is derived from evidence, never from a Status column (C-COM-005).
The productivity gain from AI-assisted development and deployment accrues to the SUPPLIER. That is a commercial position on a fixed accepted breakdown, and it is the reviewer's to take.
Estimates stay at the WBS figures. Do not re-estimate in either direction — the WBS is the customer-accepted specification (D-5).
Schedule risk is still computed against physical capacity (16 h/week), not against expected AI throughput. The two are unrelated.

An actual EQUAL to the estimate is now the expected case, not a copied-estimate smell. This reverses the prior rule; scripts/verify-worklog.py's exact-match warning is stale until reworded and should be read as informational.
Elapsed-time reconstruction (scripts/reconstruct-worklog.py) is retained for a different question — what was worked on and when — and is no longer the billing basis.
_complete_states_why_split: Reviewer decision, 2026-09-10: complete_pending_manual (built, but a required human verification step was never performed) is real for BUILD-ORDER purposes only - a successor may safely start once the predecessor's work exists. It is not billable and not acceptance-ready, because the one thing distinguishing it from true complete is exactly the missing verification that billing and acceptance exist to require. A single complete_states list let both readings share one gate and let 2.8 and 6.5 be counted as billable/acceptance-ready while sitting in complete_pending_manual. Two lists now: complete_states_build_order (wbs-ready-set.py, schedule-risk.py - 'has the work been done') and complete_states_money (compute-invoice.py, deliverable-hours.py, verify-acceptance-pack.py - 'may this be billed or accepted'). Read each script before assuming which list it needs; do not resurrect a single complete_states key.

testing_and_acceptance.live_operational_use: NONE — everything is in development (reviewer, 2026-08-19). Build Terms B5 route 3 has not fired for any deliverable.

client_testing.scope: Phase 2 as built so far — columns, views and form layout
client_testing.why_not: Handing work over to be tested is not submitting the phase for acceptance. If it were, B5's ten-business-day clock would start and silence during testing would accept the phase by default. Recorded as a V4 review, not a submission.
client_testing.verification_level: V4 — a named person opens the components and looks at them

client_acceptance.when: after the Client has tested in the acceptance environment
client_acceptance.blocked_on: promotion DEV -> TST/ACC, which is a manual step in the Power Platform Pipelines UI (ADR-007). Nothing has been promoted beyond DEV.
client_acceptance.environment: tst_acc — Test and Acceptance are one environment (TAD ADR-006)

project_start.kick_off_source: Service Agreement §03 milestone table, 'Kick-off — Project initiation meeting (complete)'. That meeting DID happen on this date; delivery did not start on it.
project_start.reviewer_statement: The project started later than expected. It only started on the 10th of August because of holidays and delay in DocuSign platform selection.
project_start.consequence: The five contractual dates did not move. 37 of the 160 calendar days between kick-off and completion — 23% — were gone before delivery began, so every phase window is compressed by that much while its deliverables and hours are unchanged.

holidays.why: Not overmacht under General Terms 10.1 (not beyond reasonable control) and not a Client access failure under 2.3. Our own scheduling.

docusign_platform_selection.basis: General Terms v1.3 clause 2.3 — 'Delays caused by the Client's failure to [provide reasonable access to information, personnel and systems] may affect agreed timescales, and the Consultant shall not be liable for any resulting delay.'
docusign_platform_selection.why_undetermined: The 20 hours of DocuSign selection and trialling were OUR work and were invoiced. Whether the delay was the Client deciding and procuring, or our own scheduling of that work, is not recorded anywhere. It decides whether clause 2.3 relief applies to part of the 37 days.
docusign_platform_selection.question_for_reviewer: Was the DocuSign selection delay waiting on Revitalise, or on us?

relief_clause.effect: Client-caused delay MAY affect agreed timescales and the Consultant is not liable for the resulting delay. It is not automatic date-shifting — it is the basis for asking.
relief_clause.note: Clause 10.1 (overmacht) does not apply to either cause.

project_start.age_basis_why: A precondition cannot meaningfully be 'open' before anyone was working on the engagement. Ages were being measured from the 2026-07-04 kick-off, which reported every long-standing dependency as 46 days old on a project 9 days into delivery. Ages now run from 2026-08-10.

build_order_constraints._purpose: Build-order edges the reviewer has directed that the customer-accepted WBS 'Depends On' column does not carry. NON-CONTRACTUAL, exactly like every other key in this file: no hours move, no deliverable changes, no task is added or removed. contract/wbs.json is GENERATED from the workbook's own Depends On column (scripts/lib/pmsources.py, read_wbs), so an edge added there would be erased by the next scripts/import-baseline.py run and reported stale by --check, and editing the workbook in place is forbidden by C-COM-009. This key is where such an edge lives when a re-approval is not available.
build_order_constraints._route_reopened_2026-09-10: When this block was written (2026-09-09) the re-approval route did not exist: the reviewer had closed it on 2026-08-19 ('WBS 0.6 is not going to come'). That decision was reversed and a client-accepted v0.6 was imported on 2026-09-10, which is what allowed the single edge here to be retired into the contract itself. A future edge should therefore ASK whether a re-approval is available before landing here - contract/README.md's routing table carries the current answer - rather than assuming this file is the only home, which is what the superseded wording above asserted.
build_order_constraints._not_a_waiver: These edges ADD a predecessor. contract/known-exceptions.json is the wrong home for them: an exception SUPPRESSES a gate that is firing, and nothing here suppresses anything.
build_order_constraints._wiring_gap: RESOLVED 2026-09-10 by docs/improvements/2026-09-10-improvement-review.md (IMP-0676, IMP-0683). scripts/wbs-ready-set.py and its .engine twin now READ this key: each edge's additionally_depends_on is unioned into the task's dependency set for readiness, and reported as 'unmet_delivery_order_dependencies' SEPARATELY from the contracted 'unmet_dependencies' so the queue never presents a delivery judgement as a contract term. Verified by execution: with 8.3 forced back to partial, it leaves the READY set and names 8.2 as a delivery-order dependency. No hand-application needed. The 'edges' array is now EMPTY - the one edge it held became contractual in WBS v0.6 and was retired on 2026-09-10 (see _retired_edges). The wiring stays, because it is what a future edge would rely on. STALE CLAIM REMOVED 2026-09-10: this note previously ended 'NOTE: 8.3 currently derives complete, so this edge does not fire today', which was already untrue when written or shortly after - 8.3 derives partial, and the edge was firing.

_retired_edges.retired_why: BECAME CONTRACTUAL. WBS v0.6, client-accepted and imported under APPROVE BASELINE on 2026-09-10, carries '8.1, 8.2' in task 8.3's own Depends On cell. contract/wbs.json now derives the edge from the accepted workbook, so keeping it here as well would state a contract term as a delivery judgement and invite a future reader to wonder which one governs. Verified before retiring: contract/wbs.json task 8.3 depends_on == ['8.1', '8.2'].
_retired_edges.retired_effect: The edge KEEPS FIRING and changes category. Measured immediately after the v0.6 import, not predicted: scripts/wbs-ready-set.py --json now reports 8.3 under blocked_by_predecessor with unmet_dependencies=['8.2'] and unmet_delivery_order_dependencies=[] - the exact inverse of what it reported while this edge lived here. 8.2 derives partial, so the predecessor is genuinely unmet either way; what changed is that 8.3's block is now a CONTRACT term rather than a delivery judgement, which is the whole point of moving it. The queue count is unaffected (8.3 was already blocked, and is still blocked).
_retired_edges.authorised_by: Xander Lykopoulos (reviewer), relayed through the plan-agent dispatch that authored docs/plans/revitalise-payment-capture-plan.md - NOT stated directly to the pm-agent dispatch that recorded it. That 'confirm before it is treated as settled' caveat is now DISCHARGED: the reviewer took the correction to the client and the client accepted it into v0.6, which is a stronger confirmation than the direct statement the caveat asked for.

WBS v0.5 gave 8.3 depends_on ['8.1'] only, so on the accepted graph the form could be built before the role that is meant to be the only thing able to see it exists - and the Bank Account and Payment columns it binds are secured under REV_FinanceOnly, whose only intended member is the REV Finance role's group team. build_order_constraints._retired_edges_why_kept: A retired edge is kept, not deleted, because the reasoning above is the only record of WHY the dependency exists - the workbook cell now carrying it says '8.1, 8.2' and nothing more. Deleting it would leave the contract stating the edge and nothing stating its cause.
